topic: hand roping a new gaff mainsail: bolt rope ease, luff length and a fluttering leech

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: dalmierz laserowy zapisujacy wymiary

base: I am hand roping a new mainsail for a gaff cutter and the luff is drawing badly.
An old storm jib in the locker was roped by the same loft thirty years ago.
A laser measure sits in my pocket and stores each luff and leech reading.
The rope seems to be pulling the cloth into small puckers every foot or so.
Have I sewn the rope too tight, or is the cloth simply gathering as it should?
Some gathering is wanted, but puckers every foot mean the rope was stretched while you sewed.
Bolt rope must be marked against the cloth first, then eased into place mark by mark.
Sewing a rope under tension shortens the luff and the sail sets in a hard curve.
Unpick a fathom, let the rope relax overnight and mark both rope and cloth again.
I unpicked two fathoms and the rope shortened by nearly three inches once it relaxed.
The laser measure gives the luff as eight point four metres along the mast track.
The old storm jib has the rope eased far more than mine, almost an inch a foot.
Is that much ease usual, or was the jib built for a much softer cloth?
An inch a foot suits old flax, which stretches under load far more than modern cloth.
Your cloth wants perhaps half that, spread evenly rather than concentrated at the head.
Mark the rope in fathoms and the cloth to match, then work from the tack upward.
Ease belongs mostly in the lower third, where the sail takes the hardest pull.
I roped it again from the tack with half an inch of ease to the foot.
The luff now lies flat and the puckers have gone entirely from the lower panels.
The laser measure shows the luff has grown by five centimetres since the first try.
Does that extra length matter on a track, or will the sail simply ride higher?
It matters, because five centimetres will put the headboard against the sheave at full hoist.
Take the difference out at the head rather than disturbing the roping you have just done.
Shorten the headboard tabling by the same amount and resew the top two seams.
Then hoist the sail dry and mark where the head actually sits against the mast.
I shortened the tabling and the head now stops two fingers below the sheave.
The sail set beautifully on a light day, with the draught well forward in the cloth.
In a fresh breeze, though, the leech began to flutter along its whole length.
Is that a fault of the tabling, or should I fit a leech line?
Fit a leech line, but only after checking that the tabling itself lies perfectly flat.
A leech that flutters everywhere usually has a tabling sewn slightly tighter than the cloth.
Lay the sail out and see whether the edge cups towards the weather side.
A line will quiet a good leech, but it cannot cure a badly sewn edge.
The tabling did cup slightly, so I unpicked it and resewed with a looser stitch.
With a leech line fitted the flutter has gone even in a good working breeze.
The sail has now had a season of use and the stitching still looks sound.
What should I watch for over the winter, and how ought the sail be stored?
Wash the salt out with fresh water and dry the sail fully before it goes away.
Roll it rather than fold it, since creases wear the cloth exactly where it bends.
Check the stitching at every corner in spring, because chafe shows there long before elsewhere.
Store it dry and off the floor, and the sail will outlast the boat's rigging.
